title: bhakti: the Chaitanya Charitamrita (selections)
hook: a minister walks out of jail to ask one question, and two Hindu schools answer it two ways
tomorrow: why would a king pick up a broom?

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti as a creeper: watered by hearing and singing, fenced against unkindness. Today, a question two schools answer two ways.

Personality quizzes promise an answer in a few clicks. Sanatana wants a real one. He's Rupa's brother, a minister to the ruler of Bengal, and he's been locked up for trying to leave his post. He pays off the jailer, crosses the forests on foot to Kashi, and falls at Chaitanya's feet. His question isn't about prison or politics. People call me learned, he says, and I believed them. But who am I?
screen: `OUT OF JAIL, ACROSS THE FORESTS.` → `PEOPLE CALL ME LEARNED.` → `BUT WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Chaitanya's answer, in paraphrase: by nature, the living being is an eternal servant of Krishna; a part of his power, one with him and also other than him, the way a ray belongs to the sun, or a spark to a fire. Hear that view at its strongest. A ray really is sunlight; it's no stranger to the sun. But it isn't the sun. That leaves room for a relationship, and a relationship leaves room for love. If there were no difference at all, who would be loving whom? In this book, bhakti isn't only something a person does. It's what a person is. Now the other answer, also from inside Hinduism, held by Advaita Vedanta, the school that follows Shankara. Its strongest case: an Upanishad says, that thou art. The self, at bottom, isn't a part of Brahman but Brahman itself; feeling like a small, separate someone is the confusion to be cleared. Hear the comfort in that. Nothing essential is ever far away. It was never other. Devotion has a place in this view too, as something that clears the mind. Both schools read the same Upanishads, and both take Sanatana's question seriously. One answers with a relationship: a ray and its sun. The other answers with an identity: a wave that turns out to be the sea. Hindu teachers still argue it, warmly.
screen: `A SERVANT, LIKE A RAY OF THE SUN.` · `ROOM FOR A RELATIONSHIP.` · `ADVAITA: THAT THOU ART.` · then, large: `A RAY AND ITS SUN, OR THE SEA ITSELF?`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and let Sanatana's question ride gently on the breath: who am I? Don't hurry an answer. Let the question rest the way sunlight rests on a floor, warm and unhurried, for the whole sit.
Bhakti, in Chaitanya's answer: not only what a person does, but what a person is, a ray made for shining.
Your line: bhakti, from the Chaitanya Charitamrita: a ray, and its sun. Two days of the book to go.

howItsDone: Gaudiya Vaishnavas teach the self as Krishna's servant, one with and different from him; Advaita Vedantins teach that the self is Brahman. Both schools study the Upanishads and the Vedanta sutras.

fork.setup: you lean toward Chaitanya's answer. a friend asks you to give Advaita's best case, fairly. which do you say?

fork.reveal: Advaita's strongest case is closeness: the separate self is the confusion, and Brahman was never far. devotion still has a place in it.

original.note: Sanskrit tat tvam asi, that thou art, from the Chandogya Upanishad; Advaita reads it as identity, other schools read it otherwise.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hinduism has one answer to who am I.
what it means: Chaitanya answers with a relationship (a servant, like a ray of the sun); Advaita answers with identity (the self is Brahman). Both read the same Upanishads.
what a scholar hears: Madhya 20, jivera svarupa haya krishnera nitya-dasa, the tatastha shakti, one and different; beside Shankara's reading of tat tvam asi, Chandogya 6.8.7.

chat.says: Sam asked if Hindus think we ARE God or SERVE God. i said 'both??' is that allowed
options: schools differ: Advaita says one with Brahman; Chaitanya's says a servant, like a ray.
tell him Hindus all agree we're God, and serving is only for beginners.
tell him Hindus all agree we only serve, and 'being God' is a myth.
chat.meaning: Chaitanya tells Sanatana the self is Krishna's servant, one and different, like a ray; Advaita says the self is Brahman.

Sanatana.meaning: Rupa's brother, a minister who became Chaitanya's student

Kashi.meaning: Varanasi, a holy city on the Ganga

Advaita Vedanta.meaning: the school that teaches the self is not other than Brahman

Shankara.meaning: the teacher whose commentaries shape Advaita Vedanta

sources.ref: Chaitanya Charitamrita, Madhya-lila 20 (Sanatana imprisoned, pays the jailer, crosses the forest, meets Chaitanya in Kashi; his questions: who am I, people call me learned; the answer: the living being is by nature Krishna's eternal servant, his marginal power, one and different, like the sun's ray or a fire's sparks)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 (tat tvam asi, that thou art), as read in Advaita Vedanta
